text: Definitely. Translation apps are great for reading a menu or asking for directions, but they can't help you build real relationships. People trust you more when you make the effort to speak their language, even imperfectly. Learning a language also trains your memory and changes how you think. Apps will keep improving, but I don't think they'll replace that human connection.

text: Children usually pick up pronunciation more easily, so starting early has clear advantages, especially if the language is used in everyday life. But adults have other strengths — they understand grammar faster and can study more systematically. So I'd say there's no age that's too late. Motivation and regular practice matter more than the age you start.

text: For the next few decades, almost certainly. English is used in science, aviation, the internet and business, and that kind of position doesn't change quickly. In the long term, Chinese or Spanish could become more important as their economies and populations grow. But I think the future is more likely to be multilingual than dominated by any single language.

text: It's very important, because a language carries a culture's history, humour and ways of thinking. In Kazakhstan, the government has invested in Kazakh-language education, and there's much more content online in Kazakh than ten years ago. I think popular culture helps most — when young people hear their language in music, films and games, they want to use it, rather than just being told they should.

text: In an ideal world, yes, because each language opens doors to new jobs and cultures. In Kazakhstan, most children already grow up with Kazakh and Russian, and English is added at school, so they effectively learn three. Adding a fourth would be too much for some students. It might be better as an option for those who are interested, rather than a requirement.
